Planned chapter

Circuit examples and the comparison with classical sampling are planned. Numerical query or runtime claims will be added with their assumptions and evidence.

Amplitude estimation extends the search components into a scalar estimation task. The chapter will connect preparation, amplification, measurement, and confidence requirements using the survey’s application perspective 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

The preparation circuit A produces a state of the formA\lvert0\rangle
=\sqrt{1-a}\,\lvert\psi_0\rangle\lvert0\rangle
+\sqrt{a}\,\lvert\psi_1\rangle\lvert1\rangle.

The task is to estimate a with a specified error and confidence level. The preparation circuit and its inverse are part of the implementation contract.

A small known-probability example with exact classical reference values.

Conventional phase-estimation-based amplitude estimation.

An iterative variant after its sampling and interval procedure is implemented.

A comparison with classical sampling of the same preparation task.

The ledger will count preparation and inverse-preparation calls, reflections, controlled operations where used, shot counts, and classical estimation. It will distinguish query complexity from compiled gate cost and physical execution time. Confidence requirements will be shared across the quantum and classical comparison.

The estimator will be tested against exact probabilities for several small instances. Coverage checks will assess the reported intervals over repeated experiments. Resource estimates will include the implemented preparation circuit rather than treating it as a unit-cost oracle.

Grover search amplifies the probability of a marked item using a reversible predicate and a reflection about a uniform superposition 

Grover, 1996. It is a useful first implementation because its circuit is small enough to inspect and its ideal success probability has a closed form. The survey gives the broader application and end-to-end complexity context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Note

Implementation status

The three-qubit demo is simulated and checked against the mathematical prediction during the site build. The generator supports other sizes. The exported circuit includes the oracle and diffuser decomposed into gates; its arbitrary rotations still require synthesis before fault-tolerant costing. The separate 

surface-code baseline records the physical assumptions and estimator output.

There are N=2^n computational basis states and exactly one marked state m. The phase oracle applies -1 to \lvert m\rangle and leaves every other basis state unchanged. Our explicit oracle compares the register to a known integer using X gates and a multi-controlled phase flip. This is a teaching example: knowing the target already solves the classical problem. A practical search application must replace it with a reversible problem predicate and count that predicate’s construction, evaluation, and uncomputation.

The notebook uses Qiskit core, an open-source circuit library released under Apache 2.0. The circuit generator is an original implementation using Qiskit core. See the 

upstream repository and the 

downloadable implementation source.

We prepare three qubits in the uniform superposition, mark integer 5 (bitstring 101), and apply two Grover iterations. Qiskit displays bitstrings with the most significant bit first; circuit wire q[0] represents the least significant bit.

The circuit below is reused directly from the saved output of the executable notebook.

n_qubits, marked = 3, 5
iterations = optimal_iterations(n_qubits)
circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
circuit.draw(output='mpl', fold=32)



Let \theta=\arcsin(1/\sqrt{N}). After r iterations, the ideal probability of the marked state isP(m)=\sin^2((2r+1)\theta).

For N=8 and r=2, this is 0.9453125. The exact statevector simulation checks this value. Sampling a real device would additionally introduce shot noise and device errors.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.bar(list(probabilities), list(probabilities.values()))
plt.xlabel('Bitstring (most significant bit first)')
plt.ylabel('Ideal measurement probability')
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.show()

Change the register size and iteration count in the browser explorer to inspect the ideal marked-state probability and the first success peak. This explorer evaluates the analytic formula. The saved figures above come from the Qiskit notebook.



Run the notebook in Binder for live Python controls that regenerate the actual Qiskit circuit and statevector. The controls support 2–6 qubits, an adaptive marked value, and 0–12 iterations. Every evaluation checks the simulated success probability against the closed form. The public notebook and its standalone implementation run independently of the private source repository.

The Binder recipe pins the scientific demo dependencies and uses Python 3.12. Its environment excludes the QDK resource estimator; physical estimates use the separate build environment and the 

surface-code baseline.

The downloadable notebook uses the same package implementation as the build script. To run the downloads independently, save 

grover.py beside 

grover.ipynb and install the scientific dependencies listed in the 

Binder environment. The 

generated metadata records the versions used by this build. From a source checkout, run:python scripts/generate_grover.py
pytest tests/test_grover.pyfrom qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
from openquantum.grover import build_grover_circuit

circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits=3, marked=5, iterations=2)
probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit).probabilities_dict()
print(probabilities["101"])
# Approximately 0.9453125

To generate a larger register without simulating its exponentially large statevector:python scripts/generate_grover.py --qubits 12 --marked 17 \
  --no-sim --no-scaling --output-dir artifacts/grover-12

Circuit generation and decomposition also consume time and memory; a large register does not imply an affordable classical simulation. The first Grover peak needs approximately \pi\sqrt{N}/4 iterations, so even constructing a fully expanded circuit grows rapidly. For estimates beyond practical expansion sizes, an independently checked symbolic cost model is a separate deliverable.

The generator transpiles the complete circuit into H, X, Z, S, T, their inverses, rotations, and CX. It records qubit width, depth, oracle calls, and the exact gate counts for the chosen Qiskit version and compilation settings. Every multi-controlled gate is decomposed before estimation. The OpenQASM 3 export contains decomposed gates and final measurements.

These logical counts are not physical qubit counts. A fault-tolerant estimate must specify rotation precision, logical error budget, code distance, state-distillation factories, timing, and failure probability. The 

surface-code baseline performs that handoff for this concrete circuit.

The scaling CSV covers 2–8 qubits with the all-ones target. It contains decomposed circuit counts rather than simulated large-register results. Changing the target changes which X gates are needed, and compilation choices can change gate counts.

The tests verify that the oracle flips exactly the requested basis state, that simulated success matches the closed form for several register sizes and iteration counts, and that decomposition preserves the unitary up to global phase. These are numerical and functional checks.

Formal proof coverage is not yet integrated. The 

SQIR/VOQC project provides relevant quantum algorithm proofs in Coq/Rocq; a linked proof does not establish correctness of this Python generator or its surface-code compilation. Any later proof badge must record the theorem, assumptions, pinned proof toolchain, successful proof build, and connection to this circuit.

The instance must state the representation of H, its coefficients and units, the error metric, and the output to be measured. Producing a state and estimating an observable will be treated as distinct deliverables.

Small optimization examples and comparative resource records are planned. No approximation guarantee or quantum advantage is claimed for the proposed examples.

This chapter will cover representative hybrid workflows: a small MaxCut problem using QAOA and a small variational energy problem using VQE. The survey supplies context for choosing application tasks and interpreting their full costs 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

For each example, specify the instance, objective, required solution quality, and the classical result used for comparison. Record both the value returned and the computational effort required to obtain it.

For a variational state \lvert\psi(\theta)\rangle, an energy objective takes the formE(\theta)=\langle\psi(\theta)\rvert H\lvert\psi(\theta)\rangle.

The ansatz, optimizer, initialization, stopping condition, and measurement procedure are part of the algorithm.

The ledger will include all optimization iterations and measurement effort, not only one ansatz evaluation. It will record classical optimizer time, parameter changes, state preparation, and any mitigation or fault-tolerant compilation used. Resource projections will keep empirical convergence observations separate from assumptions about larger instances.

Small results will be checked against exact classical optima or eigenvalues. Repeated runs will report variability from initialization and sampling. Later comparisons will match target quality and success probability and identify which quantities are measured or extrapolated.

Planned chapter

The circuits, notebooks, and numerical resource estimates for this chapter are being specified. No executed result is presented here.

The quantum Fourier transform and phase estimation are shared components for several applications covered by the survey 

Dalzell et al., 2025. This chapter will implement them as reusable circuit generators before using them inside larger algorithms.

For (N=2^n), the quantum Fourier transform maps\lvert x\rangle \longmapsto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}
\sum_{y=0}^{N-1} e^{2\pi ixy/N}\lvert y\rangle.

For phase estimation, the input includes a unitary (U) and a prepared eigenstate satisfyingU\lvert\psi\rangle=e^{2\pi i\phi}\lvert\psi\rangle.

The desired output is an estimate of \phi with a stated error and success probability. The implementation will specify bit order, the Fourier-transform convention, and how the eigenstate is obtained.

An exact small Fourier-transform circuit checked against its matrix definition.

A phase-estimation example with a known phase and an explicitly prepared eigenstate.

Parameterized generators for exact and approximate transforms.

A comparison of conventional and iterative phase-estimation variants once both are implemented.

Controlled powers of U will be charged to the estimate rather than treated as free gates. The ledger will include eigenstate preparation, controlled evolution, rotation synthesis, measurement, repetitions, and classical phase interpretation. Approximation errors will be separated from statistical failure.

Small matrices will check the transform’s convention and inverse. Known-phase examples will check the output distribution and bit ordering. Later applications will verify that their controlled-unitary construction has the claimed semantics.

The implementation and resource estimates are planned. This page defines the work required for an end-to-end factoring example.

The chapter will connect reversible modular arithmetic, phase estimation, and classical post-processing rather than presenting only a precompiled small factoring circuit. The survey provides the broader application and complexity context 

Dalzell et al., 2025.

Given an integer N and a base a coprime to N, order finding seeks the smallest positive r such thata^r \equiv 1 \pmod N.

Factoring combines sampled information about the order with classical number-theoretic processing. A complete run must include unsuccessful base choices and sampling outcomes in its success accounting.

The resource ledger will count modular arithmetic, control registers, ancillas, uncomputation, phase precision, and repetitions. It will report classical preprocessing and factor reconstruction separately. Small demonstration instances will be labeled with any simplifications that prevent their direct use as scaling estimates.

Classical modular exponentiation will check small reversible arithmetic blocks over their valid input domain. The run will verify the recovered order and factors. Register layout and ancilla cleanup will be tested before physical-resource estimates are published.

Install the versions in binder/environment.yml, or launch this notebook in Binder. To run the downloads locally, save grover.py beside this notebook. Source checkouts also work.

This pedagogical equality oracle marks a known integer. It illustrates amplitude amplification; it is not a practical classical search benchmark. Reference: L. K. Grover, A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search (1996), 

https://​arxiv​.org​/abs​/quant​-ph​/9605043. We use Qiskit core (Apache-2.0), 

https://​github​.com​/Qiskit​/qiskit.

from pathlib import Path
import sys

root = Path.cwd()
if not (root / "src").exists() and (root.parent / "src").exists():
    root = root.parent
sys.path.insert(0, str(root / "src"))

from qiskit.quantum_info import Statevector
try:
    from openquantum.grover import build_grover_circuit, expected_success_probability, optimal_iterations, decompose_to_rotation_basis
except ModuleNotFoundError:
    sys.path.insert(0, str(root / "notebooks"))
    from grover import build_grover_circuit, expected_success_probability, optimal_iterations, decompose_to_rotation_basis




n_qubits, marked = 3, 5
iterations = optimal_iterations(n_qubits)
circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
circuit.draw(output='mpl', fold=32)



probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit).probabilities_dict()
target = f'{marked:0{n_qubits}b}'
predicted = expected_success_probability(n_qubits, iterations)
print({'target': target, 'iterations': iterations, 'simulated': probabilities[target], 'predicted': predicted})
assert abs(probabilities[target] - predicted) < 1e-10



import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.bar(list(probabilities), list(probabilities.values()))
plt.xlabel('Bitstring (most significant bit first)')
plt.ylabel('Ideal measurement probability')
plt.ylim(0, 1)
plt.show()

Run the following cells in Binder or a local JupyterLab kernel to use Python controls. The published book shows saved circuit and probability outputs; its separate browser explorer computes the ideal probability formula.

The notebook controls regenerate the actual Qiskit circuit and exact statevector for 2–6 qubits and 0–12 Grover iterations. The marked value adapts to the register size. Every evaluation checks the simulated marked-state probability against the analytic formula.

import os
import numpy as np


def simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
    """Bounded ideal simulation shared by the controls and deterministic checks."""
    if not 2 <= n_qubits <= 6:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 2–6 qubits")
    if not 0 <= iterations <= 12:
        raise ValueError("Live controls support 0–12 iterations")
    marked = min(max(int(marked), 0), 2**n_qubits - 1)
    circuit = build_grover_circuit(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
    probabilities = Statevector.from_instruction(circuit).probabilities()
    expected = expected_success_probability(n_qubits, iterations)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(probabilities[marked], expected, atol=1e-10, rtol=0)
    return circuit, probabilities, marked, expected


for validation_n in range(2, 7):
    for validation_marked in (0, 2**validation_n - 1):
        for validation_iterations in (0, optimal_iterations(validation_n), 12):
            simulate_interactive_case(validation_n, validation_marked, validation_iterations)
print("Validated 30 bounded cases; every live evaluation also checks the analytic probability.")




# The book build skips widget creation so it never publishes inert controls.
# Binder and local kernels display live controls when this cell is run.
if os.environ.get("OPENQUANTUM_STATIC_BUILD") == "1":
    print("Live Python controls are available when this notebook is run in Binder or JupyterLab.")
else:
    import ipywidgets as widgets
    from IPython.display import display

    n_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=3, min=2, max=6, description="Qubits", continuous_update=False)
    marked_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=5, min=0, max=7, description="Marked", continuous_update=False)
    iterations_control = widgets.IntSlider(value=2, min=0, max=12, description="Iterations", continuous_update=False)

    def update_marked_range(change):
        marked_control.max = 2**change["new"] - 1
        marked_control.value = min(marked_control.value, marked_control.max)

    n_control.observe(update_marked_range, names="value")

    def render_live_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations):
        circuit, probabilities, marked, expected = simulate_interactive_case(n_qubits, marked, iterations)
        target = f"{marked:0{n_qubits}b}"
        print(f"Target {target}; {iterations} iterations; first-peak choice {optimal_iterations(n_qubits)}")
        print(f"Statevector probability {probabilities[marked]:.10f}; analytic probability {expected:.10f}")
        print("Ideal circuit: no device noise or fault-tolerant resource model is applied here.")
        circuit_figure = circuit.draw(output="mpl", fold=32, scale=0.65)
        display(circuit_figure)
        plt.close(circuit_figure)
        figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
        indices = list(range(len(probabilities)))
        labels = [f"{i:0{n_qubits}b}" for i in indices]
        axis.bar(indices, probabilities, color=["#1c766c" if i == marked else "#b5c6d2" for i in indices])
        ticks = indices if n_qubits <= 4 else sorted({0, marked, len(probabilities) - 1})
        axis.set_xticks(ticks, [labels[i] for i in ticks])
        axis.set(xlabel="Bitstring (most significant bit first)", ylabel="Ideal measurement probability", ylim=(0, 1))
        figure.tight_layout()
        display(figure)
        plt.close(figure)

    live_output = widgets.interactive_output(render_live_case, {
        "n_qubits": n_control, "marked": marked_control, "iterations": iterations_control
    })
    display(widgets.VBox([widgets.HBox([n_control, marked_control, iterations_control]), live_output]))

The first baseline estimates the circuit from the 

Grover chapter: initialization, the explicit equality predicate, diffusion, and final measurements. It uses the open-source 

Microsoft Quantum Development Kit and its local qdk.qre estimator. The baseline is a gate-based rotated surface code with round-based magic-state factories.

These results describe an illustrative hardware model. They do not establish an application speedup or a measured hardware performance guarantee. The equality oracle tests a known three-bit string; an application predicate or database access would need its own implementation and cost.

Every plotted point is a returned estimator result, with its physical qubit count, runtime, factory information, model properties, and instruction provenance preserved in the report. The two summary choices can coincide for a small circuit.

The three algorithm qubits do not translate into three logical compute qubits under the estimator’s scheduling model. Its logical ancillas, data code distance, and factories contribute to the physical count. These overheads can dominate a very small circuit; they are included rather than amortized over an unspecified larger workload.

For this instance, the exported rotations are exact Clifford or T operations. The QDK canonical application trace requires 28 T states and three measurements, with no arbitrary-angle rotation synthesis. The estimator abstracts Clifford work and scheduling into its resource model, so the reported runtime is a model estimate rather than an exact schedule of the original Qiskit circuit. The initial pipeline rejects arbitrary-angle traces until their approximation-error budget is specified.

Download every Pareto point as CSV · 

Download the full report as JSON · 

Download the estimated OpenQASM circuit ·

The two profiles use physical error rates of 

10-3 and 

10-4, 100 ns gate time, and 500 ns measurement time. These are editable model inputs, not benchmarks from a specific processor. The estimator explores the rotated surface-code and round-based factory model combinations and returns a Pareto frontier.

For the default example, one state is marked among eight and two Grover iterations are used. The ideal success probability per circuit execution isp_{\mathrm{success}} = \sin^2\!\left(5\arcsin(1/\sqrt{8})\right) = 0.9453125.

We set an overall failure target of 1%, reserve 0.5% for sampling failure and 0.5% for physical faults, and run two trials serially. Ideal sampling failure is (1-p_{\mathrm{success}})^2\approx0.002991. Each trial receives a physical-failure allowance of 0.25%. A union bound gives overall failure at most 0.7991% under the declared model and ideal verification assumptions. The report records the tighter bound from each returned estimate.

Peak physical qubits remain the per-trial peak because trials run serially. Runtime is multiplied by two. Quantum measurement time is included; classical verification and circuit compilation time are currently unmeasured and excluded. An application with input loading or a more complex predicate must extend this boundary before its estimate can be called end to end.

python scripts/estimate_resources.py

The project grows by completing reproducible examples within a stable chapter structure. The survey 

Dalzell et al., 2025 guides coverage; implementation order also reflects which algorithms share reusable circuit and estimation components.

Stage

Deliverable

These stages are implementation milestones. They do not imply that later families are less important or that a quantum advantage is established.

A chapter is complete when it has:

A precise task, access model, input instance, accuracy target, and success criterion.

A small circuit generated from the same implementation used for larger sizes.

A downloadable notebook and a parameterized code entry point with a pinned environment.

A check against a classical result or another independent reference.

Logical-resource accounting that includes the oracle or state preparation.

A physical-resource estimate with its code, hardware assumptions, compilation choices, and error budget.

Paper citations, software attribution, licenses, and a record of the tested version.

An incomplete item remains marked planned, partial, or unavailable. A successful small simulation does not establish scalable performance.

Early work should create components that later chapters can reuse:

Circuit generators with explicit register conventions and ancilla cleanup.

State preparation, controlled operations, and reversible arithmetic.

A common logical-resource record: qubits, operations, depth, precision, and repetitions.

A physical-estimation interface that records the model rather than hiding its assumptions.

A consistent method for saving figures, results, environment versions, and references.

The initial comparison point is a named surface-code model. Later work may change synthesis, arithmetic, scheduling, factory choices, error correction, or the application representation. Each comparison will preserve the task’s input, output, accuracy, and success requirements, then report both the resource change and the extra assumptions.

See 

resources for the baseline boundary and 

verification for evidence levels.

Each implementation should publish enough information to reproduce its small example and audit the assumptions behind larger estimates. Verification has several scopes; the page will identify which checks were actually run.

Published examples will record the input, seed where randomness is used, package versions, code revision, and command that generated each figure or result. Notebook runs should begin from a fresh kernel. Larger generators must state when construction itself becomes costly, even if simulation is intentionally limited to small instances.

The first implementation is 

Grover’s search. Its chapter describes its circuit and classical check. Other chapters remain marked planned until their artifacts and checks are available.

State-vector simulation is a useful first check for small examples. Additional methods, such as stabilizer or tensor-network simulation, will be evaluated when they fit a circuit’s structure. A simulator comparison must preserve the circuit, observables, accuracy, and measurement convention.

Every adopted simulator will be identified by package, version, configuration, and relevant reference. A link to a package will not be presented as a test result.

These links identify relevant external work. They do not establish that a proof covers this Python implementation or its resource model. A chapter will add an integrated proof artifact after its build is reproduced and its connection to the executable circuit is documented.

Each formal artifact will state:

The repository, license, revision, and toolchain.

The exact theorem and its mathematical assumptions.

Whether it covers an abstract algorithm, circuit semantics, arithmetic block, or compilation step.

The relation between the formal object and the executable implementation.

Any parts of the end-to-end pipeline outside the proof.

Current status: no reproduced formal artifact is included in this release.

The 

resource chapter defines the current model and its limitations. Later estimators will be checked for units, logical-to-physical conversion, scheduling, failure budget, and sensitivity to assumptions. Independent estimator comparisons will align their inputs before comparing outputs.

Each chapter will cite its algorithm references and any adapted code. Reused software will retain its required notices. Original narrative, third-party source code, and third-party figures will have their licenses recorded separately where necessary.

Estimates will distinguish executed results, analytical calculations, and projected values. Dates and revisions will accompany results that depend on changing toolchains or hardware assumptions.
